title_en: Guiding Case No. 227: Hu, Wang v. DeMou Restaurant, Jiang, et al. — dispute over right to life
ruling_gist_en:
1. Where a business operator, in violation of legal provisions, sells alcohol to a minor and provides it for the minor's consumption, and such fault of the business operator increases the risk of personal injury to the minor after drinking and results in damage, it shall be determined that there is causation between the illegal sale of alcohol and the personal injury suffered by the minor after drinking, and the business operator shall bear corresponding tort liability in accordance with law.

2. Where a business operator, in violation of legal provisions, sells alcohol to a minor and provides it for the minor's consumption, and a co-drinker or a person jointly engaged in a dangerous activity fails to fulfill the corresponding duty to warn and take care, causing the same damage to the minor, each shall bear corresponding several compensatory liability based on factors such as the degree of fault and the extent of causal contribution. Where the minor who suffered personal injury and his or her guardian are also at fault for the occurrence of the same damage, the liability of the tortfeasor may be reduced in accordance with Article 1173 of the Civil Code of the PRC.

full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 227

Hu and Wang v. DeMou Restaurant, Jiang, et al. — dispute over right to life

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on May 30, 2024)

Keywords

civil; right to life; minor; multiple causes leading to one result; tort liability; proportionate liability

Ruling Gist

1. Where a business operator sells alcohol to a minor and provides it for consumption in violation of legal provisions, and such wrongful conduct increases the risk of personal injury to the minor after drinking and results in damage, it shall be determined that there is a causal relationship between the illegal sale of alcohol and the personal injury suffered by the minor after drinking, and the business operator shall bear corresponding tort liability according to law.

2. Where a business operator sells alcohol to a minor and provides it for consumption in violation of legal provisions, and co-drinkers or persons jointly engaged in dangerous activities fail to fulfill their corresponding duty to warn and care, causing the same damage to the minor, they shall bear corresponding proportionate liability based on the degree of fault, the magnitude of causation, and other factors. If the minor who suffered personal injury and his or her guardian are also at fault for the occurrence of the same damage, the liability of the tortfeasor may be reduced in accordance with Article 1173 of the Civil Code.

Basic Facts

Hu A (deceased, aged 15) was the son of the plaintiffs Hu and Wang. He, Jiang (then aged 14), and Chen A (then aged 14) were second-year junior high school students at a certain middle school in Chongqing. On May 19, 2018, Hu A and others went to DeMou Restaurant in a county of Chongqing to celebrate Jiang's birthday. Hu A proposed to drink alcohol to celebrate, and Jiang agreed, so they bought beer at DeMou Restaurant and consumed it at the restaurant. After Hu A and Jiang each drank two bottles of beer, Chen A arrived at the restaurant. Subsequently, the three drank another four bottles of beer at the restaurant. After the meal, Hu A proposed to go out to play, and then they met Chen B, Deng, Zhang, and Wang A, totaling seven persons who agreed to go to a lakeside to play. While soaking feet and playing in the water at the lakeside, Hu A accidentally fell backward and drowned. Everyone attempted to rescue him but failed.

Hu and Wang sued DeMou Restaurant, the other six minors and their guardians, and the middle school, requesting joint compensation for loss of death compensation, funeral expenses, etc. It was also ascertained that the minors who dined and played together were all eighth-grade students of the said middle school; in daily teaching management, the school had fulfilled its educational responsibilities, provided routine safety education to students, and completed safety logs and teaching notes.

Judgment

The Dianjiang County People's Court of Chongqing rendered a civil judgment on March 19, 2019:

1. Defendant DeMou Restaurant shall pay RMB 21,183.36 to plaintiffs Hu and Wang;
2. The guardian of defendant Jiang shall pay RMB 3,530.56 to the plaintiffs;
3. The guardian of defendant Chen A shall pay RMB 2,824.45 to the plaintiffs;
4. The guardian of defendant Wang A shall pay RMB 1,412.24 to the plaintiffs;
5. The guardian of defendant Deng shall pay RMB 2,118.34 to the plaintiffs;
6. The guardian of defendant Chen B shall pay RMB 2,118.34 to the plaintiffs;
7. The guardian of defendant Zhang shall pay RMB 2,118.34 to the plaintiffs;
8. The middle school in Chongqing and others bear no liability.

After the judgment was pronounced, Hu, Wang, and DeMou Restaurant appealed. The Third Intermediate People's Court of Chongqing rendered a civil judgment on August 8, 2019: dismissed the appeal and affirmed the original judgment.

Reasoning

The key issue regarding whether each defendant in this case should bear compensation liability for Hu A's death is: whether each defendant, based on their roles as catering business operator, co-drinker, companion, etc., was at fault within the scope of their respective duties, and whether such fault had a causal relationship with Hu A's drowning.

1. Determination of the plaintiffs' liability.

Hu A was a second-year junior high school student at the time of drowning, had certain cognitive and judgment abilities regarding his own behavior, and had received routine safety education at school. In this case, during the dinner, Hu A actively proposed drinking alcohol, and after drinking, he engaged in dangerous behaviors such as entering the lake to play in the water, which was also proposed by Hu A himself. Hu A was greatly at fault for his own death. The two plaintiffs, as guardians, routinely tolerated Hu A's drinking, and the accident occurred during a weekend holiday. They neglected their management and education of Hu A and failed to fulfill their guardianship duties, so they shall bear 90% of the loss for Hu A's drowning.

2. Determination of DeMou Restaurant's liability.

(1) Whether DeMou Restaurant should bear tort liability for the consequence of Hu A's drowning.

Article 37 of the Law on the Protection of Minors (revised in 2012) stipulates: "It is prohibited to sell tobacco and alcohol to minors; business operators shall prominently display signs indicating that tobacco and alcohol are not sold to minors; if it is difficult to determine whether a person is a minor, they shall request the production of identification documents..." DeMou Restaurant, as a catering business operator, violated the relevant provisions of the Law on the Protection of Minors by selling alcohol to minors, which is clearly illegal; DeMou Restaurant neither carefully determined the minor status of the purchaser by requesting identification documents nor set up signs prohibiting the sale of alcohol to minors, and even allowed minors to drink in the restaurant, showing obvious fault. DeMou Restaurant illegally sold alcohol to Hu A and provided it for consumption, which objectively increased the risk of damage, and there is a certain causal relationship between the sale of alcohol and Hu A's drowning. Therefore, DeMou Restaurant shall bear tort liability.

(2) Determination of the form of liability for DeMou Restaurant.

In this case, there was no joint intent between DeMou Restaurant and the other actors before the damage of Hu A's drowning occurred, so it does not constitute a joint tort, and DeMou Restaurant does not bear joint and several liability. The sale of alcohol was not the direct cause of drowning; rather, it combined with behaviors such as entering the lake to play in the water, resulting in the damage. The single act of selling alcohol could not cause the entire damage, so DeMou Restaurant should not bear liability for the entire damage. DeMou Restaurant's illegal sale of alcohol to a minor and provision for consumption increased the risk of personal injury from entering the lake after drinking, which was an indirect cause of drowning. Considering the degree of fault and the magnitude of causation, the court decided that DeMou Restaurant bears 6% liability for Hu A's drowning.

3. Determination of liability of the six minor defendants including Jiang and their guardians.

Jiang and Chen A drank alcohol together with Hu A. After drinking, Jiang, Chen A, Deng, Chen B, and Zhang went to the lakeside with Hu A and engaged in dangerous behaviors such as entering the lake to soak feet and play in the water. The above defendants all knew or should have known that Hu A's entering the lake was dangerous. Jiang and Chen A drank with him, and Jiang, Chen A, Wang A, Deng, Chen B, and Zhang failed to stop Hu A's dangerous behavior. The above defendants failed to fulfill their mutual duty to care and warn, so they all bear liability for Hu A's drowning. Considering that Jiang was the organizer of the birthday party and participated in drinking, Chen A participated in drinking, Wang A entered the lake to rescue, and others participated in rescue in different forms, and all six defendants were persons with limited capacity for civil conduct, the court determined that Jiang bears 1% liability for Hu A's drowning, Chen A bears 0.8% liability, Wang A bears 0.4% liability, and Deng, Chen B, and Zhang each bear 0.6% liability. Since these six defendants are all persons with limited capacity for civil conduct, the tort liability is borne by their respective guardians according to law.

Furthermore, business operators who sell alcohol to minors in violation of the relevant provisions of the Law on the Protection of Minors shall also bear corresponding administrative liability according to law. After the judgment was pronounced, the people's court reminded the relevant departments by way of judicial suggestions.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Articles 1165, 1172, and 1173 of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China (applicable in this case are Articles 6, 12, and 26 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China, effective July 1, 2010)

Article 59 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Minors (applicable in this case is Article 37 of the Law on the Protection of Minors, revised on October 26, 2012)
